pedagogy.summary: This Year 5 topic explains day and night by Earth's rotation on its axis (one turn per 24 hours): your side facing the Sun is day, facing away is night, and the Sun only APPEARS to move across the sky because we are turning. The dominant challenge is the deep geocentric, 'moving-Sun' intuition built from everyday experience (Baxter's documented progression of ideas) and the frequent confusion of spin (rotation) with orbit (revolution). It is best taught by eliciting ideas first, then having children manipulate a globe and single light source — or act out the rotation themselves — while connecting the model back to real sunrise/sunset observations.
bestPractices: Elicit initial ideas first with a diagnostic probe ('what causes day and night?') to surface the 'Sun goes behind hills/clouds/behind the Earth' wrong tracks before teaching.

Use a globe and one strong light in a darkened room, with the CHILD rotating the globe (or acting as the spinning Earth) — manipulating beats watching a demo; mark 'your' location and watch it turn into and out of the light.
Explicitly distinguish rotation (spin on the axis, once a day → day and night) from revolution (orbit the Sun, once a year), because children routinely conflate them.
Reframe the apparent motion: the Sun seems to cross the sky because WE rotate; flag that 'sunrise/sunset' language reinforces the moving-Sun idea.
Sequence from a simple illumination model to the full picture and keep connecting the model to observations children make outdoors (shadows, the Sun's position).
Directly confront the 'blocking' explanations (night = Sun hidden behind hills or clouds) and the geocentric 'Sun orbits the Earth once a day'.
keyRepresentations: A globe plus a single lamp 'Sun': a marked location rotates into day and out into night.
Child-as-Earth enactment: spin to face and turn away from a lamp Sun; add walking the orbit to contrast spin with orbit.
A day/night terminator diagram — a half-lit sphere, your side vs the far side.
A spin-vs-orbit comparison: once a day vs once a year.
commonMisconceptions: Night happens because the Sun goes behind hills/mountains or behind clouds (a 'blocking' explanation).
The Sun orbits/moves around a stationary Earth once a day (the geocentric model).
The Earth orbits the Sun once a DAY to make day and night (misusing the real annual orbit).
Confusing rotation (spin) with revolution (orbit) — 'the Earth spins around the Sun in a year'.
The Sun really moves across the sky, rather than the Earth turning beneath it.
Night is caused by the Moon covering the Sun, or by Earth moving away from the Sun.

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils explain day and night by Earth's ~24-hour rotation on its axis: the half facing the Sun has day, the half facing away has night, and the Sun only APPEARS to cross the sky because we are turning beneath it. The deep obstacle is the geocentric 'moving-Sun' intuition built from everyday sunrise/sunset experience (documented by Baxter as a progression of ideas), plus routine confusion of spin (rotation, once a day) with orbit (revolution, once a year). Elicit ideas first, then have children manipulate a globe with a single light — or act as the spinning Earth themselves — and keep linking the space-view model back to their own outdoor observations of the Sun and shadows.

activities.title: Spin the Earth beside a fixed Sun — and watch the Sun 'rise'
feedback: If a learner says the Sun is travelling, pause the spin: the lamp has not moved at all — only the globe turned. The apparent motion of the Sun is the learner's own motion.

If a learner explains night as the Sun going behind hills or clouds, point to the whole half of the globe in shadow: night is the entire far side facing away from the Sun, not something passing in front of it.
Prompt them to connect back outdoors: 'When you saw the Sun low in the morning and high at midday, what was really turning?'
activities.rationale: The documented difficulty is coordinating two viewpoints — the space view of a rotating lit globe and the ground view of the Sun crossing the sky. Learner-driven manipulation (child turns the globe, or acts as Earth) rather than watching a demonstration is the recommended approach, and coupling the space view to a ground view is intended to link the perspectives that children struggle to reconcile.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 statutory 'Earth and space' requires pupils to use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the sun across the sky.

Everyday experience of the Sun rising and setting leads children to a geocentric 'moving-Sun' model; teachers should distinguish spin from orbit and have students manipulate a globe-and-flashlight model themselves rather than watch a demonstration; 'sunrise/sunset' language reinforces the misconception.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, set up one strong lamp as a fixed Sun and a globe with your own location clearly marked with a sticker.

Slowly rotate the globe yourself (don't just watch someone else) from west to east (anticlockwise when seen from above the North Pole), and track your marked spot as it sweeps from the dark side into the light and back out again.

If using a screen model: drag to spin the Earth west to east next to the fixed Sun, with a 'you-are-here' pin that sweeps from the dark side into daylight, while a coupled ground-level view below shows the Sun rise in the east, climb to its highest point around midday, then sink and set in the west, in step with your spin.
Say out loud, at the moment the Sun appears to rise in the ground view, what is actually moving — the Sun, or you?
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun did not move — YOU did. Turning the Earth is what makes the Sun appear to cross the sky, and night is simply your side facing away from the Sun, not the Sun hiding behind hills or clouds.

activities.title: Be the Earth: spin versus orbit
feedback: If a learner says 'the Earth spins around the Sun in a year', separate the two words: spinning is turning on the spot (the day); going around the Sun is the loop (the year).

If a learner claims the Earth orbits the Sun once a day to cause night, remind them that the real orbit takes about 365 days while day and night repeat about every 24 hours; have them keep spinning slowly as they walk the lap to show that many day-night turns happen during one orbit (about 365 in reality).

If a learner thinks a non-spinning Earth would still give normal day and night, point out that the daily cycle comes from the spin: with no spin, your spot would face the Sun for roughly half the year and away for the other half, so there would be no normal 24-hour day and night — only one extremely slow change across the whole year.
activities.rationale: Children routinely conflate rotation and revolution, and the recurring astronomy error is attributing day/night to a daily orbit. Acting out spin-on-the-spot versus a slow walked lap makes the distinction kinetic and memorable, and the 'stopped spinning but still orbiting' probe isolates the spin as the cause of the daily cycle.
sourceClaims: Everyday experience of the Sun rising and setting leads children to a geocentric 'moving-Sun' model; teachers should distinguish spin from orbit and have students manipulate a globe-and-flashlight model themselves rather than watch a demonstration; 'sunrise/sunset' language reinforces the misconception.
learnerActions: Stand and spin slowly on the spot facing a lamp Sun: notice your front (day) and your back (night) — one full turn is one day and night, about 24 hours.
Now, keeping facing the same direction in the room, walk a slow large loop around the lamp: this is the orbit, which takes a whole year (about 365 days).
Describe in your own words: which motion causes day and night, and which causes the year?

Try the wrong version deliberately — 'the Earth goes right round the Sun each day' — and explain why that is not what makes daytime and night-time: the real trip round the Sun takes about a year, but day and night repeat about every 24 hours.
Now imagine the Earth stopped spinning but still travelled its yearly loop round the Sun: decide whether you would still get the normal daily day and night, and explain why or why not.
activities.intendedInsight: Spinning on the axis once a day makes the daily day-and-night cycle; orbiting the Sun once a year makes the year. These are two different motions and must not be conflated — the daily cycle depends on the spin, not on the orbit.

activities.title: Elicit and confront: what causes night?
feedback: A learner can state 'day and night' correctly yet still give a wrong cause when asked why — press on the 'why' every time.
If the geocentric 'Sun travels round the Earth' answer appears, return to the fixed lamp: it did not move.
If the Earth-orbits-the-Sun-daily answer appears, return to the walked lap, which stands for the real orbit taking about a year, while day and night repeat about every 24 hours with each spin.
activities.rationale: Eliciting initial ideas with a diagnostic probe surfaces the wrong tracks before teaching, and asking for the cause separately from the surface statement separates a correct first answer from the documented underlying misconceptions. This activity is diagnostic and consolidating; recognition/selection tasks can check which misconception persists but do not by themselves build the causal-spatial model.
sourceClaims: Baxter (1989) documented a developmental progression of day/night ideas — Sun goes behind hills; clouds cover the Sun; Moon covers the Sun; Sun goes behind the Earth once a day; Earth goes around the Sun once a day; Earth spins on its axis once a day — children advancing through these with age.

Everyday experience of the Sun rising and setting leads children to a geocentric 'moving-Sun' model; teachers should distinguish spin from orbit and have students manipulate a globe-and-flashlight model themselves rather than watch a demonstration; 'sunrise/sunset' language reinforces the misconception.
learnerActions: Before any teaching, answer the probe 'What causes day and night?' in your own words and sketch what you think.
Compare your idea with the common wrong tracks: the Sun goes behind hills or clouds; the Moon covers the Sun; the Sun travels round the Earth once a day; the Earth loops the Sun once a day.
After the globe and enactment work, revisit your first answer and mark what you would now change.
Explain why, right now, it can be daytime where you are but night-time on the far side of the world — and why the Sun looks like it moves across the sky during the day.

Answer in two steps — first what happens (day/night), then WHY — choosing from the real spin explanation and the documented alternatives (Sun behind hills; Sun orbiting Earth daily; Earth orbiting Sun daily; Moon/clouds covering the Sun).
Categorise statements as 'spin (once a day)' or 'orbit (once a year)', and put a marked location in order through day → night.
activities.intendedInsight: Surfacing your own starting idea and naming the specific wrong tracks makes it possible to notice exactly which one you held and to replace it with the rotation explanation.

constraints: Learners should physically manipulate the globe or act as the Earth themselves; source guidance (NSTA) recommends this over passively watching a demonstration, which is likely a weaker way to challenge the entrenched moving-Sun intuition (comparative efficacy is not independently established here).

A static half-lit terminator diagram (tap to reveal day side / night side) is useful as a reference but cannot run the rotation or couple the space-view with the ground-view, so treat it as a support, not the main teaching.

A 3D rotatable lit Earth that zooms to the surface is vivid and genuinely spatial, but the essential perspective-coupling (space view + ground view) can also be achieved in 2D; choose based on available tools, not on an assumption that 3D is required.

Multiple-choice and categorisation tasks can check whether the misconception persists but do not by themselves elicit the independent, hands-on reasoning that builds the model; use them alongside manipulation, not instead of it.

A discussion-only (conversation) format may talk through the idea or help elicit/check a learner's thinking, but it does not itself elicit the hands-on manipulation this spatial model depends on, and there is no strong in-role persona for the day/night mechanism at this age; treat it as a weaker fit for building the model.
Flag that 'sunrise' and 'sunset' language itself reinforces the moving-Sun idea; name this explicitly when it comes up.
Keep connecting the space-view model to real outdoor observations children make (the Sun's changing position, shadows) rather than leaving the model abstract.

A physical globe and lamp are approximations: a real globe has a tilted axis and the lamp is close, so use them to show the facing/away-from mechanism, not to make precise claims about angles or distance.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (Baxter via Beyond Penguins; NSTA/IOPSpark) were marked verified:false in the source row; treat the Baxter progression and the manipulation-over-demonstration guidance as plausible but not independently re-checked here.

The source row asserted the 2D coupled model 'targets the exact misconceptions', that a static image 'will not dislodge' the intuition, and that 3D 'adds nothing essential'; these are design judgements from catalogue ratings, not established comparative efficacy, and have been softened into affordance/limit statements.
The reteach-prerequisite links (rotation/revolution and orbit prerequisites) from the assessment were not carried into learner-facing actions; they are a routing concern for the assessment layer.

The 'stopped spinning but still orbiting' answer is simplified for Year 5: strictly, an orbiting non-spinning Earth would still see the Sun's direction change once per year, so there is a very slow annual light/dark change rather than literally no change — but no normal daily cycle. Keep the emphasis on the daily cycle depending on the spin. Note too that walking a loop while keeping the same body orientation is itself the non-spinning case, which is why it is used to isolate the orbit from the daily cycle.

probeDeeper: If the Earth stopped spinning but kept travelling round the Sun, would we still get day and night? Why?
You said the Sun looks like it moves — what's actually moving? Show me with a globe and a lamp.
My friend says day and night happen because the Earth goes right round the Sun each day. What's wrong with that?
assess.correctAnswer: The Earth spins (rotates) on its axis once about every 24 hours; the half facing the Sun has day, the half facing away has night. The Sun only APPEARS to move across the sky because we are turning — the Sun is not travelling round us.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Sun travels round the Earth once a day — that's why it rises and sets' (geocentric, from sunrise/sunset language)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix a lamp as the Sun and spin the child or a globe; the moving horizon makes the fixed Sun appear to travel — the child feels the apparent motion is theirs.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun travels all the way around the Earth once a day.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes day/night to the Sun's own motion around the Earth

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the Earth goes right round the Sun once a day' (rotation↔revolution conflation — the recurring astronomy error)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate SPIN (once/24h → day and night) from ORBIT (once/365 days → the year) kinetically — spin on the spot vs walk a slow lap.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Earth travels all the way around the Sun once each day.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the Earth's orbit round the Sun causes day and night

errorPatterns.pattern: 'at night the Moon or clouds cover up the Sun' (blocking model — an early Baxter stage)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Night is the whole half of the Earth facing away from the Sun, not something passing in front of it; show the terminator on a globe.
errorPatterns.distractor: At night the Moon moves in front of and covers the Sun.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: invokes the Moon or clouds hiding the Sun to explain night

responseLevels.gap: Attributes day/night to the Sun moving round the Earth, the Moon/clouds covering the Sun, or the Earth orbiting the Sun daily.
responseLevels.full: Explains day/night by the Earth's ~24-hour rotation (facing the Sun = day, away = night), attributes the Sun's apparent motion to our own spin, and cleanly distinguishes the daily spin from the yearly orbit; transfers to 'why is it night on the far side right now?'
responseLevels.partial: Says 'the Earth spins' but cannot coordinate facing/away-from the Sun, or still mixes rotation with revolution when pressed.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Right now it's daytime here and night-time on the far side of the world. What is the Earth doing to turn our day into night? … And why does the Sun look like it moves across the sky during the day?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reason tier separates 'the Earth spins' (correct) from the documented alternatives: the Sun going round the Earth, the Earth orbiting the Sun once a day, or the Moon/clouds covering the Sun. A child can say 'day and night' correctly at tier one yet reveal any of these causes at tier two.
